task-list.what: A list of things to do, each with a checkbox so people can tick them off. Tasks often show who owns them and when they are due.
uses: Personal to-do lists and team checklists.
Showing the open steps of a project or record.
Tracking what is due this week.
avoid: Work with several stages needs a board, not a flat list.
Tasks with dependencies and dates are clearer on a Gantt chart.
practices: Group tasks by status or due date so the list is easy to scan.
Let people add a task right in the list.
Show who owns each task and when it is due.
Offer undo after a task is ticked off by mistake.
Put overdue tasks first.

kanban-board.what: A board of columns, one per stage of work, with cards that move from left to right as work progresses. It makes the flow of work visible.
uses: Team workflows with a few stages.
Support tickets, hiring pipelines or installation jobs.
Spotting bottlenecks where cards pile up.
avoid: Hundreds of cards or many columns are hard to read; use a filtered table.
Work with fixed dates is better shown on a timeline.
practices: Keep to a handful of columns with clear names.
Limit how many cards can be in progress at once.
Offer a non-drag way to move cards, for keyboard and touch.
Keep card content short: title, owner and date.
Show a count at the top of each column.

gantt-chart.what: A chart that shows tasks as horizontal bars along a time scale. It shows when each task starts and ends, how tasks overlap and how far along they are.
uses: Planning projects with dated tasks and dependencies.
Tracking rollouts or installations over weeks.
Seeing which tasks are running late.
avoid: Work without dates is better on a board or task list.
High-level plans for stakeholders suit a roadmap.
practices: Mark today with a clear line.
Show progress inside each bar.
Label late tasks with a word, not only a colour.
Order tasks so dependencies read top to bottom.
Keep the time scale short enough to read without scrolling.

roadmap.what: A high-level plan showing what is planned for which period, such as quarters or Now, Next and Later. It shares direction without promising exact dates.
uses: Sharing product or rollout plans with stakeholders.
Showing themes of work across the year.
Aligning teams on priorities.
avoid: Day-level scheduling belongs on a Gantt chart.
A single list of to-dos belongs in a task list.
practices: Use coarse periods so the plan does not promise too much.
Group work into lanes by theme or team.
Highlight the current period.
Keep item names short and in plain words.
Update it regularly so it stays trusted.

milestone-timeline.what: A line of key dates that marks important points in a project, showing which are reached and which are still ahead.
uses: Project overviews and status reports.
Onboarding or customer journeys.
Showing how far a rollout has come.
avoid: Detailed task scheduling needs a Gantt chart.
A long list of dates is better shown as a deadline list.
practices: Keep to a handful of milestones, about 3 to 7.
Show each date next to its name.
Make reached and upcoming milestones look different, and say which in words.
Point out the next milestone and how soon it is.

period-overview.what: A summary page for a sprint, month or other period. It shows the dates, the goal, progress and the work still open.
uses: Sprint pages in software teams.
Monthly plans and reviews.
Campaign periods with a goal and a deadline.
avoid: A single task list is enough when there is no goal or period.
Long-term direction belongs on a roadmap.
practices: Show days left next to progress.
State the goal in one sentence.
Count done, open and late work separately.
Let people switch to the previous or next period.
Link each number to the tasks behind it.

capacity-planner.what: A grid of people against days that shows how many hours each person is booked compared with what they can do. It makes overloaded people easy to spot.
uses: Assigning tasks or shifts fairly.
Weekly planning meetings.
Checking whether a team can take on more work.
avoid: Tracking tasks themselves is better in a task list or board.
Showing availability only is clearer in a calendar.
practices: Show each person's total against their capacity.
Flag over-allocation with an icon and words, not only colour.
Show hours per day, not only a weekly total.
Include each person's role for context.

deadline-list.what: A list of upcoming due dates, usually grouped as overdue, this week and later. It helps people see what needs attention first.
uses: Dashboards and record sidebars.
Compliance and renewal tracking.
Reminding people what is due soon.
avoid: Work with many stages is better on a board.
Events at a set time belong in a calendar.
practices: Put overdue items first and mark them clearly.
Show relative times like 'in 3 days' next to the date.
Group by urgency, not by date alone.
Keep each row to a name, a date and a state.

planning-summary.what: A summary that compares what was planned with what was done, usually as paired bars with numbers, for each team, person or category.
uses: Sprint reviews and monthly reports.
Checking whether plans are realistic.
Comparing workload across people or teams.
avoid: Trends over many periods are better shown in a line chart.
A single progress figure only needs a progress bar.
practices: Show the numbers as well as the bars.
Use outline and fill, not only colour, to tell planned from done.
Scale all bars against the same maximum.
Label each bar with a name.

plan-filter-bar.what: A bar above a plan that shows the period being viewed and the filters applied, with a count of results. It keeps the plan's current view clear.
uses: Above task lists, boards and Gantt charts.
Narrowing a plan by period, person or status.
Showing which filters are currently active.
avoid: Pages with no filters do not need it.
Many filters at once belong in a filter panel.
practices: Show applied filters as chips that can be removed one by one.
Offer one 'Clear all' action.
Show the number of results.
Keep the period control always visible.

date-range-filter-bar.what: A control for choosing a time period, with quick presets such as 'last 30 days' and a custom start and end date.
uses: Filtering reports and charts by period.
Choosing the dates of a plan view.
Setting the range of an export.
avoid: Picking a single date is simpler with a date picker.
Filtering by something other than time needs a regular filter.
practices: Put common presets first.
Always show the exact dates chosen.
Use a clear format for dates.
Reveal the custom range only when asked.

site-header.what: The bar at the top of a website with the logo, a few main links and one or two actions. It helps visitors know where they are and where to go.
uses: Marketing pages and documentation sites.
Sign-in and sign-up pages.
Public pages with a few main sections.
avoid: Inside an application with many sections, use a top bar and a sidebar.
Many links are better in a menu or footer.
practices: Put the logo at the left and link it to the home page.
Keep to about 5 links.
Mark the current page.
Make one action stand out.
Let links wrap or collapse on small screens.

top-bar.what: The bar across the top of a web application. It usually holds the menu, the logo, main sections, search and tools for the signed-in person.
uses: Every signed-in page of an application.
Giving quick access to search and notifications.
Showing the signed-in person and their menu.
avoid: Public marketing pages suit a simple site header.
Long lists of sections fit better in a sidebar.
practices: Keep it the same on every page.
Keep it low in height so content stays in view.
Move links into a menu on small screens.
Label icon-only buttons for screen readers.
Make sure text stays readable against the bar colour.

sidebar.what: A vertical list of links down the side of an application. It shows the main sections at all times and often collapses to icons.
uses: Applications with many sections.
Grouping links by area, such as admin.
Giving dense screens more room when collapsed.
avoid: Sites with only a few sections work with a top bar.
On phones, show these links in a drawer instead.
practices: Group related links under short headings.
Mark the current page.
Remember whether the person collapsed it.
Give icons text labels or tooltips.
Keep the order stable between visits.

footer.what: The area at the bottom of a page with links, legal text and company details. People look there for help, contact and policy links.
uses: Contact, help and policy links.
Legal notices and copyright.
Secondary links not in the main navigation.
avoid: Primary navigation belongs in the header.
Important actions should not hide in the footer.
practices: Group links in columns with short titles.
Include privacy and terms links.
Keep it simple and consistent on every page.
Make links big enough to tap.

page-head.what: The top part of a page's content. It tells people where they are with a title and breadcrumbs, and offers the main actions for the page.
uses: The top of every application page.
Showing the title with a short description.
Placing the main actions in a predictable spot.
avoid: Marketing pages usually use a hero section instead.
Actions for a single row belong in that row.
practices: Use one clear page title.
Show breadcrumbs or a back link to say where the page sits.
Make one action the main one.
Put the main action in the same place on every page.

messages-region.what: A fixed spot on a page where messages about the result of an action appear, such as 'Saved' or a warning. Screen readers can announce them.
uses: Confirming that a save or delete worked.
Showing errors that need attention.
Messages that must stay until read.
avoid: Short, passing confirmations suit a toast.
Errors on one field belong next to that field.
practices: Always show messages in the same place.
Announce them to screen readers.
Say what happened and what to do next.
Let people dismiss messages.
Do not rely on colour alone.

drawer.what: A panel that slides in from the edge of the screen over the page. People can do a task there while still seeing the page behind it.
uses: Navigation on phones.
Filters and quick settings.
Details of a selected row.
avoid: Long forms need their own page.
A short yes or no question suits a dialog.
practices: Trap focus inside while it is open.
Close it with Escape, the close button or a click outside.
Give it a clear title.
Return focus to the button that opened it.
Keep its content short.

top-actions-header.what: A thin row at the top of a detail or form page with a back link on one side and the page's actions on the other.
uses: Detail pages reached from a list.
Form pages with Save and Cancel actions.
Tablet and phone layouts that need little height.
avoid: Pages needing a title and subtitle need a full page head.
Navigation between sections belongs in the main navigation.
practices: Name the place the back link goes to.
Keep the actions few.
Put less common actions in a 'More' menu.
Label icon-only buttons.

settings-panel.what: A panel where people adjust how the interface looks and behaves, such as theme, density or reduced motion. Changes take effect straight away.
uses: Theme and density choices.
Accessibility preferences such as reduced motion.
Account preferences.
avoid: Rarely changed technical settings belong on a settings page.
Preferences everyone must share are project settings, not personal ones.
practices: Group related options under clear headings.
Apply changes at once and show the result.
Remember choices for each person.
Offer sensible defaults.
Use plain labels for each option.

filter-panel.what: A set of filters in labelled groups with the number of matching results. People use it to narrow a long list or table to what they want.
uses: Narrowing lists, tables and galleries.
Combining several filters at once.
Showing how many results match.
avoid: A few simple options can be a dropdown or tabs.
Free text search alone needs only a search field.
practices: Group filters under clear headings.
Show a live result count.
Offer one 'Clear all' action.
Put a search field first for long lists.
Use checkboxes for choosing several values.

filter-drawer.what: A drawer that holds a page's filters. A button opens it, people choose filters, and the results update behind it.
uses: Filtering lists, tables and galleries.
Pages with many filters.
Reports and boards.
avoid: One or two simple filters can sit above the results.
Quick sorting is better as a dropdown.
practices: Show the number of applied filters on the button.
Use a clear 'Show results' button with the count.
List applied filters above the results so they can be removed.
Offer 'Clear all'.
Open it from the same place on every page.

event-editor.what: A full form for creating or changing a calendar event, with title, date and time, repeat, place, people, reminders and notes.
uses: Creating a new event with all details.
Changing an event's time, place or guests.
Setting repeats and reminders.
avoid: Simple events can be created with a quick-add field.
Just viewing an event only needs a detail view.
practices: Put title and time first, and optional fields after.
Use sensible defaults for time, length and reminder.
Warn about conflicts without blocking save.
Keep Delete apart from Save.
Label every field.

event-popover.what: A small card that opens over the calendar when someone clicks an event. It shows the main details without leaving the calendar.
uses: Checking an event's time and place.
Quick actions such as edit or delete.
Calendar month, week and day views.
avoid: Phones have little room; use a full detail page or bottom drawer.
Long descriptions fit better in a detail panel.
practices: Keep it short: title, time, place and people.
Close it with Escape or a click outside.
Offer a link to open the full event.
Make sure keyboard users can open and close it.

event-detail-panel.what: A panel or page that shows everything about one event: title, time, place, notes, guests and actions. It has room for the full detail.
uses: Opening an event on a phone.
Showing an event from a notification or list.
A side panel next to a calendar.
avoid: A quick peek at details suits a popover.
Editing needs the event editor.
practices: Put time and place near the top.
Show guests and their answers.
Offer actions such as edit and duplicate.
Show the response bar if the person is invited.

quick-add-event.what: A single text box where someone types a sentence like 'Lunch Friday 12:00' and the event is created. It shows what it understood before saving.
uses: Adding simple events fast.
The top of a calendar or task list.
Command palettes.
avoid: Events with many details need the full event editor.
Choosing from fixed options is clearer in a form.
practices: Show the parsed date, time and place before saving.
Let people correct a wrong reading.
Link to the full editor for more options.
Give an example in the field.

reminder-manager.what: A list of upcoming reminders where people can snooze or mark them done, plus a place to set the defaults for new events.
uses: A reminders page or panel.
Notification settings for events.
Acting on reminders when they fire.
avoid: Reminders that need a message to the person belong in notifications.
Tasks with due dates belong in a task list.
practices: Make Snooze and Done one tap each.
Group reminders by when they are due.
Offer common snooze times.
Show what each reminder is for and when.

attendee-list.what: A list of people invited to an event, with their answers and a count of how many are coming. Organisers use it to see who will attend.
uses: Event details and editors.
Checking who has replied.
Adding or removing guests.
avoid: Large groups are better summarised as counts.
A single contact list is a general people list.
practices: Put the summary count first.
Show each answer as an icon and a word, not only colour.
Mark the organiser.
Let organisers add and remove guests easily.

invitation-response-bar.what: A bar on an invitation with buttons for answering, usually Yes, Maybe and No. It shows the person's current answer and lets them change it.
uses: Answering an event invitation.
Event detail views and popovers.
Pages opened from an invitation email.
avoid: Events with no invitees need no response.
Detailed replies need a form with a note.
practices: Answer in one click.
Show the current answer clearly.
Let people change their answer later.
Offer a note only after answering.

swatch.what: A small square of colour that stands for a series or a chosen colour. It links a colour on a chart to its name in the legend.
uses: Chart legends.
Colour pickers and calendar lists.
Labelling series next to a list.
avoid: Colour alone does not carry meaning; always add a name.
Different data types may need different marker shapes.
practices: Always place a text label beside the swatch.
Use colours that are easy to tell apart.
Use a line style for line series.
Keep the order the same as in the chart.

zone-swatch.what: A small mark that copies how a region is drawn on an image or video, so a list entry can be matched to its region.
uses: Lists of regions on an image or video.
Region editors.
Legends laid over images or videos.
avoid: Data series in charts need an ordinary legend swatch.
Hue alone does not carry meaning; always add a name.
practices: Match the mark to the region on the image.
Show excluded regions with a pattern, not only colour.
Place the region name beside the mark.
Keep outline and fill the same as on the image.

chart-dot.what: A small shape that marks a data point on a chart or in a legend, such as a circle, square or diamond.
uses: Scatter plots.
Markers on line charts.
Series keys in a legend.
avoid: Many points close together need a different chart or grouping.
Colour alone fails for colour-blind readers; vary the shape.
practices: Use different shapes for different series.
Keep markers a readable size.
Label each series beside its marker.
Use the same marker in the chart and the legend.

heat-cell.what: A table cell shaded from light to dark to show how large a value is. A grid of them makes patterns easy to spot.
uses: Activity by hour and day.
Occupancy or capacity grids.
Calendars showing busy and quiet days.
avoid: Exact comparisons are easier in a table or bar chart.
Data that goes above and below a target needs a two-colour scale.
practices: Print the value inside each cell.
Show a legend with the ranges.
Choose clear thresholds for the steps.
Mark empty cells differently from zero.
Add row and column headings.
